sentences: Spring light floods into the room from two directions.
In that light sits a little girl who has just been ill, gazing at a small branch in her hand.
At its tip, fresh green leaves have just begun to open.
This is The Convalescent, painted in 1888 by the Finnish artist Helene Schjerfbeck.
It is oil on canvas, 92 centimetres high and 107 centimetres wide.
It belongs to the Ateneum Art Museum, part of the Finnish National Gallery in Helsinki.
Schjerfbeck was born in Helsinki in 1862.
At the age of four she fell down a flight of stairs and injured her hip, and she walked with a limp for the rest of her life.
She could not attend school, but at eleven she was so gifted that she entered the Finnish Art Society's drawing school.
In 1880, at eighteen, she went to Paris on a travel grant.
Through the 1880s she worked in Paris, in Pont-Aven in Brittany, and in St Ives in Cornwall, painting the people and places she found there.
She painted this picture in St Ives in 1888.
She had come there after her engagement to a painter she met the year before was broken off.
For this reason, some see the painting as a kind of psychological self-portrait.
Look at the child's face.
Her wide-open eyes are fixed entirely on the branch she holds.
The brightest light in the room falls on her face and on the tiny leaves, as if both were waking up together.
Look at the branch.
Its new leaves are read as a sign of the girl's youth, or of a body just beginning to recover.
Fittingly, the painting's original French title was Premiere verdure, meaning First Greening.
Look closely at the brushwork.
The quick, lively strokes are left visible, and the handling of light recalls Impressionism.
Schjerfbeck had a gift for catching a simple everyday moment without any fuss.
The painting was shown at the Paris Salon in 1888, and the following year it won a bronze medal at the Paris World's Fair.
It was purchased for the Finnish national collection in 1888, and it hangs in the Ateneum today.
Schjerfbeck died in Sweden in 1946, after a long career that ended with spare, searching self-portraits.
In the winter of 2025 and spring of 2026, this painting travelled to New York for her retrospective at the Metropolitan Museum of Art.
Step back and see the whole room.
A child who has come through a long illness gives all her attention to a few new leaves.
Today, think about the small hope you are holding in your own hands, and the recovery it promises.
